title: The Sammy Kershaw Kerfuffle: How Red Carpets Work, And How They Could Change
summary: In this week's Billboard Country Update lead story, we talk to experts about what it's like on the red carpet.
contentText:
When the Country Music Association presents its 60th annual awards on Nov. 18, nine-time nominee Ella Langley , seven-timer Miranda Lambert and five-timer Kacey Musgraves all have the potential for a big night.

Who seemed to get the most attention in the run-up to the awards?

So far, that would be Sammy Kershaw, an artist who hasn’t had a top 10 single in 28 years and has just one CMA nomination — a 1993 nod for the Horizon award — in his history. In a single social-media post on Nov. 6, less than two weeks before the awards, he lamented that he’d been “strung along for months,” only to discover that he would not be allowed to walk the red carpet. The Kershaw kerfuffle generated criticism from the general public, which mostly perceived the decision as a slight to an older artist. Rodney Atkins, Stella Parton and The Frontmen Live — Tim Rushlow, Larry Stewart and Richie McDonald — subsequently revealed similar interactions with the CMA, and artists such as Riley Green, Clay Walker, Pam Tillis and Jake Owen voiced support and/or sympathy for Kershaw.

The drama placed the trade organization in a tough position. It’s in the CMA’s best interest to have a positive relationship with every artist in the genre, and it’s generally accepted that the trade organization will never say anything negative about any performer. But the carpet — as glamorous as it might appear on a TV at home — is actually a high-stress, high-priced work environment that’s utterly chaotic, no matter how much effort goes into planning. Even if the CMA wanted to accommodate him, Kershaw represents just one member in a class of artists that’s problematic for some other red-carpet participants, all of whom use the carpet for different purposes.

While plenty of fans have seen red-carpet coverage on TV, most consumers — and, probably, the majority of the industry itself — have never actually experienced one in person. Carpets involve three different camps: the awards show; the artists, along with their teams; and the media. For a balanced understanding of the controversy, the Billboard Country Update talked with two people who have worked in two of those three areas: Triple 8 manager Scott Stem, a former CMA publicist who now manages Scotty McCreery; and TriStar Southern Hills Medical Center director of communications Jesse Knutson, who previously covered red carpets as a reporter for WTVF-TV Nashville and organized them as an Academy of Country Music publicist.

The primary purpose for the carpet is to generate publicity for the show. Both the CMA and ACM typically spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to create the setting. Those costs include building rental, the physical carpet, ropes, stanchions, lights, staff, backdrops, WiFi and other electronics. With that investment, the organization puts a sharp priority on creating PR for the telecast, both to drive viewership and to create post-show buzz. And the artists most capable of doing that are the most prominent acts.

“They have a limited amount of time and a limited amount of space,” Stem says, “and the first priority for them with a red carpet are the artists who are involved in the show — the nominees, the presenters, and the performers.”

Both organizations have typically allowed former winners and artists with current hits on the carpet, since their stories can help with that engagement, but it gets complicated with artists outside that scope. Many of the national media is focused strictly on a handful of acts related to that show and resist talking to new acts or heritage artists. Meanwhile, plenty of smaller outlets and country-centric media are willing to speak with just about anyone, in part because of the interview’s future value. Some reporters develop non-awards stories by polling artists on the carpet, others end up with game-like content or short pieces about individual performers. Still others gather selfies for social media or use the time to build relationships with newer artists. Many of those developing acts fade away, but some become major stars, and the content becomes more valuable.

“How many clips have you seen of reporters interviewing Taylor Swift , like on her first red carpet?” Knutson asks rhetorically. “Those come up from time to time, but you don’t know who’s going to be the next Taylor Swift until they become Taylor Swift.”

To the casual observer, it appears that the artists arrive randomly, though there’s a flow to the schedule. The show’s participants have a dress rehearsal in the afternoon, and they tend to appear in the final hour or two once they’re done with that practice run. The first hour or two of the carpet are the most ideal for the acts who are not involved with the production, and the awards show team tries to slate artists so that they arrive at a steady pace, though it never goes exactly as planned. To some degree, setting that schedule is comparable to assigning tables at a wedding reception.

“I tried to plan them so Ella Langley would walk at a similar time to Riley Green when their big song came out together,” Knutson says. “If I knew that people had fun relationships, like Maren Morris and Brothers Osborne , [I put them] on the carpet at a similar time. Keeping Blake Shelton and Miranda Lambert apart — we did that, too.”

The carpet’s first hour is typically slow, particularly for the media at the end of the line, who may have to wait for 10-20 other media to conduct their abbreviated, three-minute conversations before the artist reaches them. But by the end of the carpet’s schedule, artists are stacked up, often standing along a backdrop at the edge of the carpet waiting for other artists to finish their interviews. Meanwhile, reporters are often looking down the line as they conduct interviews, plotting who might be coming, fearing that the biggest artists will walk past them.

It’s potentially brutal to an artist’s ego, and the artist’s team typically preps the performer in advance that not every outlet will be appropriate for them.

“That’s just kind of the law of the jungle out there,” Stem says. “You have to understand how that works.”

Kershaw and the CMA came to an agreement, and the singer is now expected to walk the carpet. Thanks to the controversy that came from it, Kershaw will be one of those acts that most media will want to interview, but in the long run, organizations may allow the already-cramped carpets to become even more crowded to avoid potentially bad publicity. For this particular year, Kershaw’s carpet walk may not fit the original goals for any of the parties involved.

“Every single reporter,” says Knutson, “is going to be asking him about this, not about the show, and not about whatever projects he’s working on.”
